title: 1 Kings 17:1–7
context: The Elijah cycle opens abruptly after the report that Ahab married Jezebel of Sidon, served Baal, and provoked the LORD more than the kings before him (1 Kings 16:31–33). Elijah the Tishbite announces in the LORD’s name that there will be neither dew nor rain except at his word, a judgment that recalls the covenant warning that idolatry would shut up the sky (Deuteronomy 11:16–17). The LORD then sends him to hide by the brook Cherith, whose exact location is uncertain, where ravens bring him bread and meat until the brook dries up. The New Testament remembers this drought as an answer to Elijah’s earnest prayer (James 5:17). Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the passage as shared ground about the LORD’s rule over the rain that Baal worship claimed for itself, and about his faithful care for his servant.

verses.text: Elijah the Tishbite, who was one of the settlers of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah standing boldly before Ahab and announcing the drought in the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. His prayer and obedience are real factors in the story, as James 5:17 emphasizes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the drought as the LORD’s covenant judgment on Baal worship, since the rain belongs to him, not to Baal (compare Deuteronomy 11:16–17). Readers in both traditions commonly hold that God answers prayer as part of his good purposes.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came to him, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the LORD’s word comes to Elijah right after his bold announcement. The prophet does not plan his own next step but waits for God’s direction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD guiding his servant step by step through his word. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a reminder that God leads those who serve him.

verses.text: “Go away from here, turn eastward, and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, that is before the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God telling Elijah to hide by the brook Cherith, east toward the Jordan. Obedience sometimes means withdrawal rather than confrontation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD protecting his prophet from Ahab’s anger by sending him away. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the exact location of the brook Cherith with caution.

verses.text: You shall drink from the brook. I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that God has commanded the ravens to feed Elijah. Provision comes from an unexpected and unclean source, showing God’s freedom to care for his servants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s command over creation, even ravens, as a picture of his providence (compare Psalm 147:9). Both traditions commonly read the verse as assurance that God provides what he calls his servants to need.

verses.text: So he went and did according to the LORD’s word, for he went and lived by the brook Cherith that is before the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah going and doing according to the LORD’s word. Trusting obedience is the response God seeks from his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Elijah’s obedience as the fruit of faith in God’s promise. Readers in both traditions commonly hold up the verse as a simple model of faith that acts.

verses.text: The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening; and he drank from the brook.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the ravens bringing bread and meat morning and evening, with water from the brook. Daily provision teaches daily dependence on God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see an echo of the manna given each day in the wilderness (compare Exodus 16:4). Both traditions commonly connect this provision with Jesus’ teaching to ask for daily bread (Matthew 6:11).

verses.text: After a while, the brook dried up, because there was no rain in the land.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the brook dried up because there was no rain. Elijah shares in the hardship his own announcement brought on the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the drying brook as God’s way of moving Elijah to the next stage of his plan. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a test of trust when familiar provision ends.
